summary: This RFC defines a Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588-2019) profile for IPv4 or IPv6 enterprise networks. It uses the end-to-end delay measurement mechanism and allows both multicast and unicast Delay Request and Delay Response messages, so clocks across an enterprise can be synchronized in a common way.

plainLanguage.summary: Lots of clocks in a building need to show the same time exactly. This tells them which of the possible ways of asking and answering to use so they agree.

subtitle: A PTP profile that lets big enterprise networks mix multicast and unicast for precise clock sync.

tldr.problem: PTP was built around multicast, so in large networks most devices receive and throw away messages meant for someone else, and PTP has so many options that vendors struggle to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The Enterprise Profile fixes the options: Sync and Announce go out as multicast, Delay Request and Delay Response may be multicast or unicast, end-to-end delay measurement is mandatory, and several optional features are forbidden.
tldr.outcome: Devices from different vendors can be configured the same way to deliver common precise time across an enterprise network. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9760 is a Proposed Standard from May 2025. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of the Enterprise Profile.

sections.title: Why an Enterprise Profile
sections.content:
Large enterprise networks, such as those in financial corporations, increasingly need distributed time-tagged measurements like one-way packet latencies. That needs a common precise time on many devices. The text says the financial industry requires accuracy from 100 microseconds to 1 nanosecond to the Grandmaster. This profile sets no timing performance requirements itself, but those needs are why NTP as commonly implemented often cannot meet them.

The original Precision Time Protocol (PTP, IEEE 1588) used only multicast. In domains with many nodes, devices had to discard most received multicast messages, and the RFC cites a figure that the share discarded as irrelevant can exceed 99%. A PTP Profile narrows PTP's many options so equipment from different vendors interoperates, and this one was demonstrated at the ISPCS Plugfest.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a stadium hears every announcement meant for one person, they waste effort ignoring it. This profile lets some messages go to just one person.

sections.title: Clock Roles and Terms
sections.content:
The RFC uses the optional IEEE 1588g terms timeTransmitter (instead of master) and timeReceiver (instead of slave). The Grandmaster is the timeTransmitter currently acting as the reference time source of a PTP domain, chosen by the Best TimeTransmitter Clock Algorithm.

An Ordinary Clock has a single PTP Port in a domain. A Boundary Clock has more than one PTP Port, typically one timeReceiver port and others that redistribute timing. A Transparent Clock measures how long a PTP event message takes to cross it and adds a correction. A domain is a separate PTP system, and every PTP message carries a domain number.
sections.plainLanguage: One clock is the boss of time, others copy it, and some in-between clocks pass the time along and note how long it took.

sections.title: Message Transport and Delay Measurement
sections.content:
The profile works only over UDP on IPv4 or IPv6. The End-to-End delay measurement method MUST be used. TimeTransmitters, Transparent Clocks and Boundary Clocks MAY be one-step or two-step clocks, and timeReceivers MUST support both.

  • Sync messages MUST be multicast PTP event messages on UDP port 319, sent to the PTP primary address.
  • Two-step clocks MUST send Follow-up messages, and Announce messages MUST be sent, as multicast general messages on UDP port 320.
  • The primary address is 224.0.1.129 for IPv4 and FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:0:181 for IPv6.
  • Delay Request messages MAY be multicast or unicast. A timeTransmitter MUST answer a multicast request with a multicast Delay Response, and a unicast request with a unicast one.

Because the unicast option lets timeReceiver Only Clocks that lack Enterprise Profile support take part, the profile can serve very large numbers of timeReceivers.

PTP assumes the one-way delay for Sync and Delay Response messages is the same, so the network SHOULD be engineered so forward and reverse paths match. Clocks SHOULD support multiple domains so that several timeTransmitters can provide redundancy.
sections.plainLanguage: The time is shouted to everyone, but when a clock asks how long the shout took, the answer can come back privately, only to that clock.

sections.title: Default Message Rates
sections.content:
Sync, Announce and Delay Request default to once per second, and these defaults MUST be used. Sync and Delay Request rates MAY be changed, but not to less than once every 128 seconds and not to more than 128 messages per second. The Announce rate MUST NOT be changed.

The Announce Receipt Timeout Interval MUST be three Announce Intervals for Preferred timeTransmitters and four for all other timeTransmitters.
sections.plainLanguage: By default each clock chirps once a second, and a clock is declared silent after missing a few chirps in a row.

sections.title: Requirements for Each Clock Type
sections.content:
TimeTransmitters MUST follow the standard Best TimeTransmitter Clock Algorithm, though several Grandmasters may be active if each is in a different PTP domain. A port MUST NOT be in the timeTransmitter state unless the clock has a current value for the number of UTC leap seconds. Unicast negotiation signaling messages MUST be ignored.

TimeReceivers SHOULD use time from all timeTransmitters in multiple domains, MUST work even if they use only one domain, and MUST operate properly in the presence of a rogue timeTransmitter. They SHOULD NOT synchronize to a timeTransmitter that is not the Best timeTransmitter in its domain. Because Transparent Clocks can replace the source IP addresses of Sync and Follow-up messages, timeReceivers MUST send Delay Requests to the IP address found in the Announce message.

Transparent Clocks MUST NOT change the transmission mode of a message, for example turning unicast into multicast. Boundary Clocks SHOULD support multiple domains and MUST NOT combine timing information from different domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of clock has its own job rules. Followers should not obey a pretender, and in-between clocks must not change how a message was sent.

sections.title: Forbidden Options and Interoperation
sections.content:
Clocks in the profile MUST NOT use peer-to-peer delay measurement, Grandmaster Clusters, the Alternate timeTransmitter option, Alternate Timescales, unicast discovery or unicast message negotiation. They MUST also avoid any optional feature that requires Transparent Clocks to alter Announce messages, since that would stop timeReceivers from finding the timeTransmitter's protocol address.

Management messages MAY be used, but those aimed at a specific clock MUST be unicast; signaling messages meant for one node MUST also be unicast. The profile interoperates with the IEEE 1588 Default Profile in Annex I.3 (end-to-end delay) when it runs over IPv4 or IPv6 and uses unicast management for specific clocks, but not with the Annex I.4 variant that needs peer-to-peer delay measurement. The profile identifier is 00-00-5E-01-01-00, profile number 1, version 1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Some fancy features are banned so every clock plays by the same simple rules and they can all work together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Time protocols matter for security mechanisms that use time windows for keys and authorization, and time passed through a network can be manipulated. Using multiple simultaneous timeTransmitters in multiple PTP domains can mitigate rogue timeTransmitters and on-path attacks such as delay, interception and manipulation attacks, since failures would have to happen on more than one path at once.

PTP management messages SHOULD NOT be used because they lack a security mechanism; secure management can come from mechanisms such as NETCONF (RFC 6241). Further security mechanisms are outside the scope of the document, which points to RFC 7384 for general time-protocol security. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Using several time sources that take different routes makes it hard for a trickster to fool every clock at once.
